title: The interacting galaxy pair NGC 1512 and NGC 1510
caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 1512 and NGC 1510, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Two galaxies in the constellation Horologium, NGC 1512 and its smaller neighbor NGC 1510, take center stage in this image, caught in the act of interacting.
NGC 1512 has been merging with NGC 1510 for 400 million years. That long, slow interaction has set off waves of star formation and bent both galaxies out of shape.

When galaxies interact, their gravity pulls on each other's stars and gas. Clouds of gas get compressed, and compressed gas is where new stars form, so encounters like this often trigger bursts of star birth. The same forces can distort a galaxy's disc, twisting or warping it. Over enough time, a smaller galaxy can be absorbed entirely by a larger one, and mergers of this kind are thought to be one of the main ways galaxies grow.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the pair through g, r, i, z and Y filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
